questions.q: What is the standard anatomy of a data quality check query, per this lesson?
options: SELECT key columns, FROM the table, WHERE the condition is true only when the row is bad
SELECT *, FROM the table, WHERE the condition is true only when the row is good
INSERT the bad rows into a log table, then DELETE them from the source
UPDATE the bad rows to a default value, then SELECT the result
questions.explain: The lesson's core pattern selects just enough key columns to identify a bad row, filtered by a WHERE clause written for the failure condition, not the success condition.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend writing the WHERE clause for the failure condition rather than the success condition?
options: A check's purpose is to find rows that need attention, not to confirm rows that are already fine
SQL Server only allows WHERE clauses that evaluate to false for good rows
Writing a success condition is always slower to execute
It's required syntax for UNION ALL queries
questions.explain: A check query is meant to surface problems. Selecting the bad rows directly (rather than the good ones) is both the more useful output and the habit the lesson recommends building.

questions.q: What does UNION ALL accomplish in the combined 'failures report' pattern?
options: It combines multiple rules' violations into a single result set, each labeled with which rule fired
It removes duplicate rows across all the combined queries
It automatically fixes the data quality issues found
It converts all column data types to VARCHAR automatically
questions.explain: UNION ALL stacks the results of multiple independent rule-check queries into one result set, each branch contributing a RuleName and RecordKey so every violation is identifiable and reviewable together.

questions.q: What does it mean for a WHERE clause to be "SARGable", and why does it matter?
options: The condition is written so the query engine can use an index on it, rather than wrapping the indexed column in a function
The condition only works on string columns, never on numeric columns
SARGable queries can never use a JOIN
It means the query runs only in SQL Server Agent jobs, not in SSMS
questions.explain: A SARGable condition (e.g. OrderDate >= '2024-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-01-01') lets the engine use an index on OrderDate, unlike wrapping the column in a function like YEAR(OrderDate), which forces a full scan.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say checks should be kept strictly read-only?
options: A check's job is to detect problems; fixing them (remediation) is a separate, deliberate step covered later in the course
SQL Server does not allow UPDATE or DELETE statements inside stored procedures
Read-only queries always run faster than any UPDATE statement
Only database administrators are allowed to write UPDATE statements
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes detection (checks, this chapter) from remediation (fixing the data, covered in Chapter 5) — mixing the two risks unintended changes from what should be a safe, repeatable audit query.
